questions.q: Why isn't a SIEM alert, by itself, proof of a real incident?
options: Alerts only fire after an incident has already been fully resolved
Alerts are always false positives by default
SIEMs are incapable of generating accurate alerts
An alert is a claim that something bad might be happening, which Detection & Analysis must confirm or rule out
questions.explain: This lesson frames an alert as a claim, not a fact — Detection & Analysis is what closes that gap with real evidence.

questions.q: How does Detection & Analysis relate to the alert triage process taught earlier in this path?
options: It only applies to alerts that have already been dismissed as false positives
It replaces triage entirely and ignores raw log data
It has no relationship to triage at all
It's the same validation discipline applied at incident scale, with higher stakes for getting it wrong
questions.explain: Detection & Analysis builds directly on the fire-review-classify-act triage loop, now applied to confirming a full incident.

questions.q: Besides confirming an alert is real, what is the other job of Detection & Analysis?
options: Writing the final post-incident report
Immediately isolating every affected system regardless of type
Assigning blame to the employee involved
Understanding the incident's nature, since the correct response differs by incident type
questions.explain: Confirming an incident is real is only half the job — understanding its nature determines the right response.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why might a quietly compromised user account need a different response approach than active ransomware?
options: Compromised accounts are never a real security concern
A careful, quieter response avoids alerting the attacker and causing them to destroy evidence
There is no meaningful difference in how either should be handled
Ransomware always requires less urgency than a compromised account
questions.explain: The lesson contrasts ransomware's need for aggressive isolation with a quiet compromise's need for careful handling.

questions.q: What happens when a team is too slow or too skeptical to confirm a genuine incident?
options: The incident is automatically reclassified as a false positive
The SIEM automatically escalates the alert to law enforcement
Nothing changes, since dwell time only applies during Containment
The attacker's dwell time grows, since they continue operating undetected
questions.explain: Dwell time, introduced in SOC Operations & SIEM Fundamentals, keeps growing the longer a real incident goes unconfirmed.
